 The 11th hour: How Armistice Day became Veterans Day 
 Bill Rubin | Opinion Columnist

 4 hrs ago 
 0

 No mail delivery. No in-person banking. Federal offices are closed. States observe holidays differently. Ever think about how a national holiday came to be? 
 Glancing at this month’s calendar, the St. Croix Valley’s know-it-all did a little thinking about how Nov. 11 came to be Veterans Day. It took some work, but the know-it-all is a better person, and his thin resume is now padded with “subject expert.” 
 Armistice Day, then Veterans Day 
 At the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918, a ceasefire took effect between Germany and the Allies of World War I, which included the U.S. Fighting and bloodshed continued right up to the appointed hour of 11 a.m. Oddly, the ceasefire did not end the war. The Treaty of Versailles was signed June 28, 1919. 
 The word “armistice” may be old and worn. It means an agreement between warring parties to stop fighting, though a legal state of war still exists. In World War I, fighting stopped Nov. 11, and the peace treaty came seven months later. 
 President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed the first Armistice Day on Nov. 11, 1919. In 1938, Congress passed legislation making Nov. 11 a legal federal holiday honoring World War I veterans. Veterans groups later pushed for change. In 1954, Congress amended the 1938 act, replacing “Armistice” with “Veterans” and broadening the tribute to veterans of all wars. President Dwight Eisenhower, himself a veteran, signed the amendment. 
 Memorial Day and Veterans Day both honor the military, but they remember different groups. Memorial Day honors service members who died serving their country. Veterans Day pays tribute to all military veterans, living or dead, who served in wartime or peacetime. 
 Programs honor veterans 
 Across the St. Croix Valley, there are numerous opportunities to honor veterans Nov. 11. Many programs start at 11 a.m. — remember, it’s the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month. Ceremonies follow a familiar pattern: color guard, invocation, speaker, singing, bands, a three-volley rifle salute and, of course, taps, the mournful 24-note bugle call. Some service groups offer free breakfasts, others lunch, and all offer veterans a chance to connect. 
 Who is a veteran? 
 Today’s veterans are diverse, representing every race, ethnicity, gender and economic background. They’ve settled into civilian life as heads of households, educators, first responders, lenders and elected community leaders. Veterans likely won’t mention their service. They are the proverbial men and women next door. Don’t overlook “citizen soldiers,” regular citizens who serve in military reserve and National Guard units. Weekend drills and the dreaded deployment are stark realities. 
 Veterans in the St. Croix Valley 
 An estimated 5,047 veterans live in St. Croix County, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. That’s about 5% of the county’s population. Women make up about 9% of the county’s veterans, roughly 472. Pierce County is home to a little more than 1,900 veterans, or 4.5% of its population. Women make up about 6%, a little more than 120. Veterans are aging. More than 1,000 St. Croix County veterans, about 20%, are 75 or older. In Pierce County, roughly one-third of veterans are 75 or older. 
 The know-it-all ends with a request: Regardless of age or gender, let’s remember veterans Nov. 11. A toast heard in saloons and taverns puts it in perspective: “To the living; to the fallen.” Here’s to our veterans.
